---

The family-wide contract for the **next-phase offer**: the guidance every pipeline command
surfaces at the end of its run, naming the natural next command(s). Cited by all pipeline
commands so the routing graph and the offer rules live in ONE place (the same shape as
`emit-block` in `feedback-emission.md`).

## The offer contract (7 rules)

1. **Guidance-only** — the offer NAMES the next command(s); it NEVER auto-invokes anything. **One exception, operator-elected:** an option the operator picks from the offer itself may run the command it names, as a complete run of its own — today only `/product-workflows:brd-split`'s *Ground now*, which runs `/product-workflows:prd-ground` on the children the operator chooses, after the split's pull request has merged (that command's *Ground now — the operator-elected continuation*). Nothing runs unless that option is chosen, the merge stays the operator's act, and every other option of every offer stays guidance. It exists because the operator would otherwise retype a command whose arguments the run already holds, with no decision between the two runs that the offer could not ask.

2. **Role-labeled** — it names the concrete command(s) for the next step, tagged with the owning
   role (PM / PA / PE / Dev / Security Engineer), even on a handoff — one person may wear several hats and just keep
   going. Never a bare "hand off to PA".

3. **Adaptive to outcome** — a clean run points forward; a BLOCK / incomplete / cancelled run
   recommends resolving THAT first, not advancing.

4. **Mode-aware** — the forward recommendation is a PIPELINE handoff. In a command's direct /
   ad-hoc mode (no PRD/Epic context — `/dev-workflows:implement` direct, `/docs-workflows:document` doc-edit) it is OMITTED,
   not invented.
5. **Epic fan-out** — a command operating at **Epic scope** offers TWO branches (and `/dev-workflows:implement` names more before them: each follow-up task its Phase 1 printed and the run answered, to tick once its change merges, then one for each other code repository it recorded a change for — the run from that repository, addressed to the unit it implemented, the Epic itself where it was one):
   - **Depth** — the next command for the SAME Epic (`/dev-workflows:design <EPIC>` → `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>`).
   - **Breadth** — the SAME command for the NEXT Epic under the PRD (`/dev-workflows:design <EPIC-1>` →
     `/dev-workflows:design <EPIC-2>`).

   So a team can go `/dev-workflows:design E1 → /dev-workflows:design E2 → /dev-workflows:implement E1 → /dev-workflows:implement E2` OR
   `/dev-workflows:design E1 → /dev-workflows:implement E1 → /dev-workflows:design E2 …` — their call. Applies to the per-Epic commands
   only: `/product-workflows:create-ard <EPIC>`, `/product-workflows:specify <EPIC>`, `/dev-workflows:design <EPIC>`,
   `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>`. `/docs-workflows:document` and `/docs-workflows:release-notes` are PRD-level (whole-feature, run
   once after ALL Epics are implemented) and do NOT fan out.

6. **Fully qualified when printed** — every command name the run PRINTS for the user to invoke is
   written `/<plugin>:<command>`, fully qualified with the plugin that ships it. A bare `/<command>` can resolve to a Claude Code built-in of
   the same name — Claude Code's own `/release-notes`, `/upgrade`, `/statusline` and `/feedback` all
   collide today, and the built-in wins; its `/design`, which makes a Design artifact, collides on the
   accounts it is switched on for — so the bare form is NEVER printed. Prose that describes the
   pipeline to a reader of the family's own source keeps the short form.

7. **One address, never a pair** — every offer prints exactly ONE positional address, because every
   keyed command takes exactly one (D4: a key encodes its own ancestry, so an Epic address is all an
   Epic-scoped run needs and the PRD is derived from the folder above it). An offer written
   `/product-workflows:specify <PRD> <Epic>` names an argument form no command accepts: the run reads the
   first token, and the second either disagrees with it or is refused. Write `/product-workflows:specify
   <EPIC>` for an Epic-scoped step and `/product-workflows:specify <PRD>` for a PRD-scoped one — the
   prefix of the folder the address resolves to is what sets the altitude, and a folder with none is
   placed by what it holds (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/addressing.md` §4.1), so the offer
   never has to say it twice.

**The remaining Epics are named.** Where a lane line of the routing graph says "the remaining Epics", the printed offer never writes that phrase bare, nor a placeholder where a key belongs. It names each other Epic folder directly under the PRD folder by its key, one address each (rule 7) — the folder listing is the set, never a key read out of a resume pointer, a report or a carry-forward line, and each name it prints is held to `workflows-core:addressing` §2's class before its key, its `implementation.md` or its `epic.md` is read, a folder outside it that may be an Epic folder named by its position with its remedy in place of a step, as §2's *A folder refused by its name* says, `<P>` the PRD folder's path — with the state the run can see of it: `no implementation record` where its folder holds no `implementation.md`; `implemented — not merged` where the run applied `workflows-core:implementation-format` §5's merged test to each repository's latest block in its `implementation.md`, as *A unit's work is merged* takes them in that §5, and the test did not show the Epic's work merged; and otherwise `implemented — merge not checked`. An Epic that test showed merged is not a remaining one and is left out. Each gets its next step. For one with no implementation record it is `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>` — rule 5's breadth where the offering command is `/dev-workflows:implement`, and the same step from `/dev-workflows:conformance` and `/security-workflows:scan` — where the Epic's `specification.md` and `design.md` are both on the default branch, or, on a specs tree that is no git repository, in the Epic's folder, and otherwise, in its place, what that Epic's first missing document needs (the Dev lane's *`/dev-workflows:implement` precondition*). For one implemented, it is what the Dev lane's `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>` line names before that Epic's pull request merges — `/dev-workflows:conformance <EPIC>`, then `/security-workflows:scan <EPIC>` from each repository its `implementation.md` names, each beside the record its folder already holds of it (`_conformance.md`, `_security.md`) where it holds one — and then that pull request's review and merge. The offer orders them, the run's own pull request among them, by the PRD-level ARD's `### Landing order`, the list as the PRD folder's `ard.md` writes it — the same list `workflows-core:ard-resolution` returns as `landing_order` — each Epic placed where its `epic.md`'s `target:` stands in it. Where this Epic's own pull request has still to merge and a remaining Epic's target comes before this Epic's, the offer says that this Epic's pull request merges after that Epic's has. Epics whose targets stand in one place keep key order, and the offer asserts no order between them; where the PRD folder holds no `ard.md`, the ARD has no `### Landing order`, or an Epic has no `target:` or one the list does not name, the offer asserts no order for that Epic and says no recorded order places it. Where the run's unit is the PRD folder itself — a PRD implemented, traced or scanned as one unit — every Epic folder under it is a remaining one, and the unit's own pull request is placed by no target. Where no other Epic stands under the PRD, or every other one was shown merged, the offer says so and names none.

**A next-step offer that names a downstream command must also name the merge.** The downstream command executes `require-on-main` (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §3) and stops while this phase's pull request is open, so an offer that reads "next: `/product-workflows:create-ard <KEY>`" without "once the pull request is merged" sends the user into a stop they were not warned about.

So the merge is named by every next-step offer that names a downstream gate its own run feeds. **An offer that names none does not**, and `/product-workflows:brd-proposal` is the case: it hands off an artifact no `require-on-main` gate targets — a later run of that same command reads it, which is a read and not a gate — and its own next-step options name no gate its run feeds, so it carries no clause anywhere — which is why the rule is stated against the gate the offer names rather than against membership of the `/product-workflows:brd-*` family, whose glob it matches. `/security-workflows:scan` is the same case: its register is bookkeeping, which no pull request hands off and no `require-on-main` gate targets, so none of its offers carries a clause. This reference ships in `workflows-core`, which prints no next-phase offer of its own: `/workflows-core:frames` makes only its handoff offer, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §4.3's consent choice (*Not pipeline nodes*), and that offer carries no clause on purpose: nothing runs `require-on-main` on a frame-set index, so no downstream gate reads what it writes. `/product-workflows:create-ard`'s prose offer of `/product-workflows:harvest-decisions` carries the clause too, though that command runs no `require-on-main`: it reads only the default branch, so an ARD not yet there is not harvested, and the clause names that wait.

**And an offer that names the merge must name it truthfully, which means the clause is never unconditional.** A run that staged nothing — save where `phase-handoff.md` §2.3 re-publishes a reused branch, whose push row is then the line — or whose handoff the user declined, opened no pull request — and "once the pull request above is merged" then parks the operator waiting for a merge that will never happen, on a run they could often start immediately. Worse, the failing outcomes differ from each other — of those two, only one has a branch to name, and they are not the only two §4.1 defines. So an offer carries the clause as the placeholder **`<merge-clause>`**, resolved from the `Phase handoff:` line `phase-handoff.md` §4.1 actually emitted. **Where a run emitted more than one — §4.1 names the producers that do: `/brd-reconcile`, and `/dev-workflows:design` and `/product-workflows:specify` where their *Next Epic* loop hands off more than one Epic — the clause resolves from the line reporting the handoff of the artifact the offered command's gate targets**, which is the run's own deliverable rather than any ancillary one it also landed — on a *Next Epic* loop, the line of the Epic the offer names; for `/brd-reconcile`, `/brd-package` and `/prd-ground` — and, through `decisions.md`, `/create-prd`, `/create-ard` and `/specify` — gate on what the reconciliation record's handoff carried, not on the canonicalised customer review:

| §4.1 outcome | `<merge-clause>` resolves to |
|---|---|
| Committed, pushed, PR opened | `(once the pull request above is merged)` |
| PR already existed | `(once the pull request above is merged)` |
| PR not opened | `(once you open the pull request for <branch> and it is merged)` |
| Push failed | `(once <branch> is pushed, its pull request opened, and merged)` |
| Push refused for access | `(once <branch> is pushed — this identity may not push to origin — its pull request opened, and merged)` |
| No remote | `(once <branch> is merged into the default branch — this specs repo has no remote, so no pull request will do it)` |
| Nothing to commit, the deliverable already on `<default>` | `(its inputs are already on the default branch — you can run it now)` |
| Nothing to commit, the deliverable on `<current>`, unmerged | `(its inputs sit on <current>, unmerged — it waits until <current> reaches the default branch)` |
| Nothing to commit, the deliverable changed on `<default>` after `<current>` was cut | `(the default branch changed its inputs after <current> was cut — merge the default branch into <current>, or run it from the default branch)` |
| Nothing to commit, the deliverable changed on `<default-ref>`, which the local `<default>` is behind | `(the default branch changed its inputs since your local copy of it — pull <default>, then run it)` |
| Commit failed | `(once the deliverable staged on <branch> is committed, pushed and its pull request merged)` |
| Declined by the user | `(once this run's artifacts reach the default branch — they are written but not there)` |
| Gate failed | `(once this run's artifacts reach the default branch — the handoff did not run)` |
| Switch refused | `(once <branch>'s pull request is merged, or it is closed and <branch> deleted, and this run's artifacts reach the default branch)` |
| Anything else, or unresolvable | `(once this phase's artifacts are on the default branch)` |

`Branch name substituted`, `Stacked on another phase's branch`, `Declaration unaccounted for` and `Record unreadable` are appends to another line rather than outcomes of their own — whatever branch the emitted line ends up naming is the branch the clause names. A *Nothing to commit* line can name two — the branch this run cut, removed or kept, and `<current>`, the branch it stands on, where the deliverable sits — and its clauses name `<current>`, never the cut branch. **The table resolves every outcome row of §4.1 that is not an append, and the catch-all is for a line that could not be read at all** — never for an outcome §4.1 defines. Twice it fell short of that, and each omission dropped something the run was holding: at first *PR already existed* fell to a catch-all that never named the pull request the operator has to merge, and *No remote* to one that never named the local branch the artifacts are committed on; later *Commit failed*, added to §4.1 without a row here, fell to one that never named the branch its deliverable is staged on. **Which rows name a branch is the point**: §4.1's declined and gate-failed lines carry none, because on those paths `handoff-to-main` left nothing on a branch, so there is no branch to send anyone to — where *No remote* commits, on a branch that exists and that nothing in that repository will ever push, and *Commit failed* stages the deliverable on a branch it cut, so each is exactly a row that must name one. Count the branch-naming rows off the table rather than off this sentence, and check a row added to §4.1 against it: the property is *left something on a branch* — committed or staged — and a row added without a branch where the run left something on one is the defect this paragraph exists to catch.

**Where the placeholder sits in the text, which is a convention of its own and stood in one adopter rather than here.** It never goes inside the code span that carries the command. In prose it takes a span of its own, after the command's — `/product-workflows:specify` and `/dev-workflows:design` write it that way — and in a `choices:` option it is plain text, which is how `/product-workflows:update-prd` writes it in both its offer box and its array. **The reason is the table above**: every value the placeholder resolves to is a parenthesised English sentence, so a clause inside the command's span makes the one line an operator copies end in a positional token of prose — and on an offer that *is* that one line, nothing beside it marks where the command ends. Inside an option it follows the command, its address, and any role or `(Recommended)` label; a purpose clause may follow it in turn, as `/product-workflows:brd-reconcile`'s *Package again* option does, so "last token of the option" is the common shape and not the rule. **Re-derive it rather than trusting this paragraph** — `grep -rn '<merge-clause>' plugins/*/commands/*.md`, and read each hit for whether the token sits inside a span that also holds a command — a `choices:` array quoted whole in one span aside; today none does, in prose or in an array. The test is the placeholder's own span and never the option's: an option may legitimately carry a code span for something else, and a few do.

**Resolving this placeholder is not a rewording.** The array is still presented verbatim per `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/escalation-rules.md`'s *Choice lists are presented verbatim*, exactly as `<BRD-KEY>` or `<KEY>` is substituted in the same strings. A command that instead told the orchestrator to *adjust the wording* of an option would be contradicting that convention, which is why the variation lives in a placeholder and not in an instruction.

## Surface

The universal minimum is an adaptive **`### Next step`** section at the END of the command's
Final Report (guidance-only prose). A command MAY additionally present a richer interactive
`choices:` offer (the reference commands `/product-workflows:idea`, `/product-workflows:create-prd`, `/product-workflows:create-ard` do) — compatible,
not required.

**When there are more forward options than the array can hold.** `AskUserQuestion` renders at most
four options (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/escalation-rules.md` §0), and several offers have
more forward steps than that. The prose is what carries the complete set — it is the universal
minimum precisely because it has no arity limit — so an overflowing offer resolves like this, and
never by silently deleting a route:

1. **List every option in the prose**, above the prompt, each with the command that runs it. A route
   named in prose is a route the operator can still take.
2. **The array carries `Stop here` plus the three the run's own outcome makes most likely**, in the
   same order the prose lists them. Rule 3 (adaptive to outcome) is what decides "most likely"; where
   a command already drops options on their own triggers, that filtering runs first and the cap
   applies to what survives it.
3. **Say, in one line, that the prose list is longer than the prompt** and that anything on it is
   reachable through the harness's free-text option. A demoted route the operator cannot find is the
   same defect as a deleted one. **Put that line where the dialog shows it, naming every route the
   array leaves out** — each with the command that runs it, in the prose's order, after
   `Not shown as an option:` — because a run can skip the prose it prints before a prompt, and a
   line in the prose would then point at nothing. It goes in the question's own text; where an
   array carries an option naming the rest, it goes in that option's `description` instead, the
   rule `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/epic-picker.md`'s *The cap* states for a picker built
   from a listing. No option's label sends the operator to the prose list.

An offer whose options fit in four does none of this: the prose stays the universal minimum and the
array carries every option.

## The routing graph (role-aware)

**Every `/product-workflows:epics` option the routing graph names is conditional on the folder it names
holding an authored `prd.md`** (`kind: prd`): `/epics` accepts a PRD folder or an `EPIC-` folder
under one and refuses everything else (`/product-workflows:epics` Phase 0 step 1b). `/epics` also
stops while that `prd.md` is on no ref or only on an unmerged branch, and after a revision it stops
on the difference or reads the default branch's earlier copy, without the revision, until that
revision is merged (its Phase 0, *Gate the PRD*), so an offer of it by a run that has just written
or edited the PRD carries `<merge-clause>`. Where the
caller's PRD folder — the resolved folder itself on a PRD-level run, its parent on an Epic-level
one — holds no `prd.md`, which the BRD route reaches legitimately since `/product-workflows:create-prd`
is not a prerequisite for `/product-workflows:create-ard` there, the offer is
`/product-workflows:create-prd <PRD>` instead, `<PRD>` being that tested folder's own key and
never an Epic's — save where that folder holds the PRD under its pre-rename file name (the test
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §4.4's `prd.md` rung makes), on which
`/product-workflows:create-prd` would write a second PRD: there the offer names the rename, never
`/product-workflows:create-prd`, as §4.4's *The first missing document* names it, through
`/product-workflows:specify <PRD>`, whose own stop prints the rename's commands, saying that run
stops — **and only where `/product-workflows:create-prd` can itself run**: it refuses more than one shape —
three on the BRD route, and an `EPIC-` folder on either, which is why the key is the PRD folder's
— so on a BRD-route slice the slice's ledger tests are read first, and each offering command
names what `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §4.4's *The first missing document*
names for them at its `prd.md` rung, which restates them for a plugin that cannot read their
authority, `product-workflows:coverage-ledger-format` §5.2 — a naming, as that rung is, never a stop
that applies them, which is `/product-workflows:create-prd`'s own, taken in its Phase 0; where the
slice's `brd-link.md` names no `parent:`, which that rung reads first, no option at all, the offer
printing in its place the rung's no-`parent:` line; and where they fail the offer resolves to what the
failing outcome names: `/product-workflows:brd-split` against one of two keys; no option at all
where none applies — the gate set non-empty and no row `covered-here`, the offer saying where the
requirements went, or the gate set empty and the parent's ledger unreadable, that ledger reported by
path; and, where the slice's `coverage-ledger.md` is missing or unreadable while `claims:` names
rows, no option either, the file reported by path and `/product-workflows:prd-ground <PRD>` named
beside the dropped option, in prose, never as an option or `(Recommended)`, as the run whose stop
tells an interrupted carve from a lost file and names the repair, saying it stops there by design.
Where the caller's PRD folder holds a `prd.md` asserting no `kind: prd`
— which `/epics` reads as no PRD and `/product-workflows:create-prd` counts as found, offering
`/product-workflows:update-prd` or an overwrite — the offer names neither: in their place it says
that the file asserts no `kind: prd`, and that adding the `kind: prd` and `key: <PRD>` its format
carries (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/addressing.md` §5) is what lets
`/product-workflows:epics <PRD>` read it, once that edit is merged to the default branch or, on a
specs tree that is no git repository, once it is made — where the offer is an option of a
question, the option left out and that said in the question's own text. An offer whose run stops the moment it starts is the same defect the
`<merge-clause>` rules exist to prevent, one command further on: a next step the operator
cannot take from the state the report describes.

**Dev — build, verify & deliver**

**The `/dev-workflows:implement` precondition.** `/dev-workflows:implement <KEY>` stops on arrival where the unit it builds — the Epic's folder on an Epic's address, the PRD folder on a PRD's address with no Epic folder under it, and, on a PRD's address with Epic folders, the unit its picker settles, which leaves out every Epic lacking either file and stops where nothing is left — lacks its `specification.md` or its `design.md` on the default branch (`/dev-workflows:implement` Phase 0, *Gate the unit's specification and design*; `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §3.4). So every offer of it in this lane is conditional. Where the offering run has just written or annotated a file of the unit's pair, the offer carries `<merge-clause>` for it, as every offer of a command whose gate its run feeds does (*A next-step offer that names a downstream command must also name the merge*). Every other file of the pair must already be on the default branch for the offer to name the command — `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" cat-file -e "<default-ref>:./<path>" 2>/dev/null` exiting 0 for it, or, on a specs tree that is no git repository, the file in the unit's folder — and where one is not, the offer names in its place what the unit's first missing document needs (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §4.4, *The first missing document*), as that run's own stop would. On a PRD's address with Epic folders the offer names the command where at least one unit that run would offer — an Epic, or, on a PRD that is not multi-component, the PRD folder's own broad slice — holds both and holds no implementation record, since that run asks before it implements a unit already built (`/dev-workflows:implement` Phase 0); otherwise it names in its place what each Epic lacking either file needs first, and the broad slice's where the PRD folder's `specification.md` is written, as `/dev-workflows:implement <PRD>`'s left-out lines name them, and nothing where none lacks one — save an offer to fix a unit's built work, as `/security-workflows:scan`'s on a finding is, for which a unit holding both is enough. A direct `/dev-workflows:implement`, which resolves no unit, has no such condition.

- `/dev-workflows:design <EPIC>` → optionally `/dev-workflows:ready <EPIC>` (verify readiness) →
  `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>` — each `<PRD>` in place of `<EPIC>` after a broad PRD-level
  design, whose Epic is null: the next address is the folder the design was written into.
- `/dev-workflows:ready <ADDRESS>` → **SUPPORTED** → `/dev-workflows:implement <ADDRESS>` (the same address) where the unit's `specification.md` and `design.md` are on the default branch, or, on a specs tree that is no git repository, in the unit's folder — a condition `/dev-workflows:ready`'s Phase 1 has already read for each unit it located — and otherwise, in its place, what the unit's first missing document needs (*`/dev-workflows:implement` precondition*) — SUPPORTED judges the phase the artifacts reach, not that the pair is there; **PARTIAL / NOT-SUPPORTED**
  → resolve the named gaps, then re-run `/dev-workflows:ready`. Whatever the verdict, a PRD at
  *Implementation* or later whose delivery is not verified → PE → `/dev-workflows:conformance <PRD>` (PE, every
  Epic merged), whose settled record verifies it — lifting a PRD at *Implementation* to the optional *Delivery verified* rung. *(Read-only verifier;
  not itself a linear pipeline node — an optional gate before build.)*
- `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>` → first, where it answered a follow-up task its Phase 1 printed, each such task to tick once its change merges, and, where it recorded a change another code repository needs, the run from that repository, addressed to the unit the run implemented (the Epic itself, where it was one); then, before its pull request merges, `/dev-workflows:conformance <EPIC>` and then `/security-workflows:scan <EPIC>` (Dev), from the repository that run branched — the fixes from either return to `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>`, which continues on the Epic's branch (`workflows-core:implementation-format` §5); then the remaining Epics (breadth), each named and placed with this Epic's pull request in the ARD's landing order (*The remaining Epics are named*); once ALL Epics implemented and merged →
  PE → `/dev-workflows:conformance <PRD>` → `/docs-workflows:document <PRD>` → `/docs-workflows:release-notes <PRD>`. *(Direct mode → no forward offer.)*
- `/dev-workflows:conformance <EPIC>` (Dev, before its pull request merges) → a `fix-code` decision → `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>`, which continues on the Epic's branch while its pull request is open, then `/dev-workflows:conformance <EPIC>` again — `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>` only where the Epic's `specification.md` and `design.md` are on the default branch, or, on a specs tree that is no git repository, in the Epic's folder, and otherwise, in its place, what its first missing document needs (*`/dev-workflows:implement` precondition*); none → where the run traced the Epic's branch before the merge (its `after_merge` false), `/security-workflows:scan <EPIC>` (Dev — a key run is the `dev` role's scan) from each repository whose branch the run traced before the merge, then the pull request's review and merge and the remaining Epics, ordered together by the ARD's landing order (*The remaining Epics are named*); then the PE's `/dev-workflows:conformance <PRD>` — the whole route after an Epic run that traced no branch before the merge, its pull request having merged.
  `/dev-workflows:conformance <PRD>` (PE, every Epic merged) → a `fix-code` decision → `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>` (`<PRD>` where the PRD has no Epics), only where that unit's `specification.md` and `design.md` are on the default branch, or, on a specs tree that is no git repository, in that unit's folder, and otherwise, in its place, what its first missing document needs (*`/dev-workflows:implement` precondition*); an `amend-document` decision → the command its note names — `/product-workflows:update-spec <KEY>` only where `<KEY>`'s `specification.md` is on the default branch (on a specs tree that is no git repository, none: the note's change is made by hand there) and, on a `PRD-` slice or an Epic under one, the slice's `brd-link.md` names a `parent:` — where it names none, the no-`parent:` line of `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §4.4's *The first missing document* in its place, since that run stops there — and `/product-workflows:create-ard` or `/product-workflows:epics` only where the PRD folder's `prd.md` is (on a specs tree that is no git repository, in its folder), and otherwise, in its place, what that document needs (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §4.4, *The first missing document*), save `/product-workflows:create-ard` on a BRD-route slice, whatever its `prd.md`'s state, for which that rule's `prd.md` rung reads the slice's ledger tests first — `/product-workflows:create-ard` where the slice's `brd-link.md` names a `parent:`, they pass and its `prd.md` needs no landing, one that is nowhere being no gap there, and otherwise, in its place, what the rung names — and `/product-workflows:epics` where the folder holds no `prd.md`, or one asserting no `kind: prd`, for which the *`/epics` precondition* names what stands in its place; or `/dev-workflows:design <KEY>` for a `[DT#N]`, which takes no note; once settled → `/docs-workflows:document <PRD>`.
  Either run, each threat, stand-alone design entry or stand-alone ARD Rule its `### Threats` lists → Dev → `/dev-workflows:design <KEY>` for `unanswered — no design answers it`, a `[DT#N]` decided *Amend the document*, a stand-alone entry that is `unreadable`, a stand-alone entry that is `unanswered — returned to the architect` and stands alone because `it answers no live threat with a deferred part` or because `its threat is in no model a refine reads beside this design`, and a threat that is `unanswered — returned to the architect`, on each design that returned it, after the PA's route below, since each refine puts that threat again until the Dev answers it again there; PA → `/product-workflows:create-ard <KEY>` for `stale`, `review due` and a threat that is `unreadable`, and for `unanswered — returned to the architect`, save those two stand-alone entries, `unanswered — no design takes it` and `open` on a decision the team will not build — each, on a BRD-route slice or an Epic under one, on the terms the `amend-document` decision's `/product-workflows:create-ard` takes there above, since the run printing these lines names what `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/phase-handoff.md` §4.4's *The first missing document* names in place of each of its offers of that run: `/product-workflows:create-ard` where that rule's `prd.md` rung finds the slice's `brd-link.md` naming a `parent:`, its ledger tests passing and its `prd.md` needing no landing, and otherwise, in its place, what the rung names; the scan after an Epic run with no `fix-code` decision stays.
- `/security-workflows:scan <EPIC>` (Dev, before its pull request merges) → a `fix` decision → `/dev-workflows:implement <EPIC>` (continues on the Epic's branch; only where the Epic's `specification.md` and `design.md` are on the default branch, or, on a specs tree that is no git repository, in the Epic's folder, and otherwise, in its place, what its first missing document needs: *`/dev-workflows:implement` precondition*), then the pull request's review and merge — where the scan ran under `after_merge`, whose pull request has merged already, the review and merge of the pull request that run opens; after the merge, `/security-workflows:scan <repo-path> --verify-fixes` (Security Engineer; register `security/<repo-slug>/`); none → the pull request's review and merge — none under `after_merge` — and the remaining Epics, ordered together by the ARD's landing order (*The remaining Epics are named*), then the PE's `/dev-workflows:conformance <PRD>`. Either way, `/security-workflows:scan <EPIC>` (Dev) from each other repository the Epic's `implementation.md` names, since a change scan reads the repository it is run from; and, where accepted risks are past their review-by date or decisions await security review, `/security-workflows:scan <repo-path> --triage` (Security Engineer; register `security/<repo-slug>/`).
- `/docs-workflows:document <PRD>` (PRD-level, after all Epics) → `/docs-workflows:release-notes <PRD>`. *(Doc-edit mode → no
  forward offer.)*
- `/docs-workflows:release-notes <PRD>` (PRD-level) → leaf/closure: release note drafted; continue any pending
  PA/PE phase, else the PRD is fully processed.

## Session hygiene co-fires here

The `### Next step` this contract produces is immediately followed by a
`### Context hygiene` block (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/session-hygiene.md` §2): the compact-vs-clear
choice reads the SAME role labels computed here (same role → `/compact`; role handoff →
`/clear`). This reference owns the role graph; `session-hygiene.md` only reads it.
